marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q001.takeaway: The trans-tubercular plane joins iliac-crest tubercles and crosses the upper border of L5.
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q001.displayText:
The trans-tubercular plane joins iliac-crest tubercles and crosses the upper border of L5.

The structures marked in red are the tubercles of the iliac crest. An imaginary line passing through them forms the trans-tubercular plane, which lies at the upper border of L5.

The abdomen is divided into nine regions by two transverse planes and two vertical planes. The subcostal plane joins the lowest points of the costal margins and corresponds to the 10th costal cartilage and lower border of L2/upper border of L3. The trans-tubercular plane joins the iliac-crest tubercles and corresponds to L5. The right and left lateral planes run from the midclavicular point to the mid-inguinal point.
emphasis: The trans-tubercular plane joins iliac-crest tubercles and crosses the upper border of L5

rationales.a: Lower L3 is too superior for the iliac-tubercle plane.
rationales.b: Upper L4 is above the standard L5 level.
rationales.d: Lower L5 is below the upper-border landmark.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q003.takeaway: The marked gallbladder fundus lies at the transpyloric plane, approximately L1.
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q003.displayText:
The marked gallbladder fundus lies at the transpyloric plane, approximately L1.

The structure marked X is the fundus of the gallbladder. It lies at L1 in the transpyloric plane.

The tip of the ninth costal cartilage in the transpyloric plane, near the junction of the linea semilunaris with the costal margin, is used to identify the gallbladder fundus. The transpyloric plane lies midway between the suprasternal notch and upper border of the pubic symphysis and crosses the lower half of L1 posteriorly.
emphasis: The marked gallbladder fundus lies at the transpyloric plane, approximately L1

rationales.b: L2 is below the usual transpyloric-plane level.
rationales.c: T11 is too superior for the fundus landmark.
rationales.d: T12 lies above the L1 plane.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q004.takeaway: The pancreas is retroperitoneal (except its tail) and commonly refers pain to the back.
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q004.displayText:
The pancreas is retroperitoneal (except its tail) and commonly refers pain to the back.

The pancreas is retroperitoneal; the other listed structures are intraperitoneal. Pain from retroperitoneal organs is likely to be referred to the back.

The source table classifies viscera by peritoneal relationship, including stomach, jejunum/ileum, transverse and sigmoid colon, liver/gallbladder, and spleen as intraperitoneal; abdominal esophagus, D2/D3 duodenum, pancreas, kidneys/ureters/adrenals, abdominal aorta/IVC, and celiac plexus as retroperitoneal; and ascending colon, descending colon, and rectum as partially covered/secondarily retroperitoneal in the source table.
emphasis: The pancreas is retroperitoneal (except its tail) and commonly refers pain to the back

rationales.a: Jejunum is intraperitoneal and not the likely retroperitoneal source.
rationales.b: Most of the liver is intraperitoneal, aside from its bare area.
rationales.c: The stomach is intraperitoneal, not the likely retroperitoneal organ.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q006.takeaway: The mesorectum contains the superior rectal vein, accompanying vessels and lymphatics within the excised mesorectal envelope.
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q006.displayText:
The mesorectum contains the superior rectal vein, accompanying vessels and lymphatics within the excised mesorectal envelope.

The mesorectum is excised in total mesorectal excision and contains the superior rectal vein.

The rectum has no mesentery, but is surrounded by fat enclosed within a fascial envelope called the mesorectum. It contains the superior rectal artery and branches, superior rectal vein and tributaries, lymphatic vessels, and nodes. Anterolaterally, branches of the inferior hypogastric plexus and middle rectal vessels enter the mesorectum within a fascial layer called the lateral rectal ligament.

Total mesorectal excision is a standard procedure for rectal cancer and removes tumor with surrounding fatty tissues, vessels, and lymphatics in the mesorectum.
emphasis: The mesorectum contains the superior rectal vein, accompanying vessels and lymphatics within the excised mesorectal envelope

rationales.a: The superior mesenteric plexus is not a content of the mesorectum.
rationales.c: Inferior rectal veins drain the anal canal/perineum, not the mesorectal envelope.
rationales.d: Inferior rectal artery supplies anal canal and is outside the mesorectum.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q008.takeaway: The medial umbilical fold overlies the obliterated umbilical artery (medial umbilical ligament).
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q008.displayText:
The medial umbilical fold overlies the obliterated umbilical artery (medial umbilical ligament).

The structure marked X is the medial umbilical fold. It overlies the obliterated umbilical artery.

The lower anterior abdominal-wall peritoneum is raised into five folds: a single median umbilical fold extending from umbilicus to bladder apex and containing the urachus/remnant; paired medial umbilical folds extending toward the umbilicus and overlying obliterated umbilical arteries; and paired lateral umbilical folds overlying inferior epigastric vessels.
emphasis: The medial umbilical fold overlies the obliterated umbilical artery (medial umbilical ligament)

rationales.a: The urachus remnant lies in the median umbilical ligament, not the medial fold.
rationales.c: Inferior epigastric vessels form the lateral umbilical folds.
rationales.d: The median ligament runs from bladder apex to umbilicus; the obliterated umbilical arteries form paired medial folds.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q009.takeaway: The caudate lobe forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen, so an instrument advanced there may injure it.
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q009.displayText:
The caudate lobe forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen, so an instrument advanced there may injure it.

The superior border of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe of the liver and is likely to be injured in this case.

The epiploic foramen is a vertical slit about 3 cm long behind the free right border of the lesser omentum connecting the lesser sac with the greater sac.

Clinical note: the Pringle maneuver compresses the free margin of the lesser omentum to rapidly control bleeding from the hepatic artery and portal vein in liver trauma and surgery.
emphasis: The caudate lobe forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen, so an instrument advanced there may injure it

rationales.a: Right hepatic lobe lies lateral to the foramen rather than its superior boundary.
rationales.b: Quadrate lobe is inferior to the porta hepatis, not the roof of the foramen.
rationales.d: Gallbladder fundus is anterior/inferior and not adjacent to the superior margin.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q010.takeaway: The paraduodenal recess is associated with the inferior mesenteric vein in its free margin.
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q010.displayText:
The paraduodenal recess is associated with the inferior mesenteric vein in its free margin.

The paraduodenal recess contains the inferior mesenteric vein in its right free margin.

The source explains that folds around D4 and the duodenojejunal junction form several named recesses, probably from minor developmental aberrations of duodenal rotation and fixation.
emphasis: The paraduodenal recess is associated with the inferior mesenteric vein in its free margin

rationales.a: The superior duodenal recess is near the duodenojejunal flexure but not the IMV-bearing fold.
rationales.c: The inferior duodenal recess is a separate peritoneal pocket.
rationales.d: The mesentericoparietal recess is not the one whose free edge contains IMV.

marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q011.takeaway: In a supine patient, free intraperitoneal fluid commonly collects in the right subhepatic hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch).
marrow__ANAT_CH48_Q011.displayText:
In a supine patient, free intraperitoneal fluid commonly collects in the right subhepatic hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch).

The most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position is the right subhepatic space (hepatorenal pouch of Morison), where intra-abdominal fluid collects.

It lies between the inferior surface of the right lobe of liver and upper pole of right kidney. Boundaries: superiorly, inferior layer of coronary ligament; inferomedially, hepatic flexure, transverse mesocolon, second part of duodenum, and part of pancreatic head; laterally, right lateral abdominal wall; posteriorly, anterior surface of upper pole of right kidney.

In erect posture, the most dependent part is the rectovesical pouch in males and rectouterine pouch in females.
emphasis: In a supine patient, free intraperitoneal fluid commonly collects in the right subhepatic hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch)

rationales.a: Right infracolic space is lower and separated from upper spaces by mesocolon.
rationales.b: Left infracolic space is not the most dependent upper abdominal recess when supine.
rationales.d: Left paraduodenal space is not the usual dependent fluid collection site.
